paras: The threatened lynching of Wyatt Jones took place in August 1885 near Lynchburg, Harris County, Texas, when residents hunted Jones, a Black man accused of raping a white girl, intending to lynch him. Jones was instead captured by two Black men and brought to the Houston jail, where the sheriff was expected to hold him to keep him out of the townspeople's hands.

About August 6, 1885, a girl near Lynchburg, named in dispatches as Miss Northcoutt and given as 16 years old, was reported to have been raped and found unconscious. A Houston dispatch placed the alleged assault on the bank of the San Jacinto River.

Jones fled, and on August 7 the San Antonio Light reported that Lynchburg would "have a lynching bee" if "the excited populace" could run him down. According to a Houston special, "the people of Lynchburg" hunted him for a week "to lynch him." About August 13 he was caught near Stafford's Point, some twenty-five miles from Houston, by a Black man. Two Black men then brought him into Houston at 2 o'clock in the morning, tied to a horse, and turned him over to the sheriff.

Interviewed in jail, Jones said he was innocent and that he had run away because he feared being lynched over a suspicion that he had committed adultery. The Houston correspondent added that he had been "fully identified" as the man charged.

Sheriff Fant was expected to hold Jones in Houston for examination, fearing he would be lynched if sent to Lynchburg. No report of an examination, trial or later fate for Jones appears in the coverage found.

Only white papers carried the case: a State News brief in the San Antonio Light, a Houston special in the Dallas Daily Herald that the Dallas Weekly Herald reprinted on August 20, and a separate Houston dispatch printed in Tombstone, Arizona. The Dallas Herald called Jones "a negro brute" and stated the rape as fact, while still noting that he "denies the crime." The Tombstone dispatch, headed "Strapped to a Horse," wrote that he was "charged with" the crime and gave his own explanation for fleeing. None of the papers commented on the planned lynching, and no Black-press account was found.

The first report named the accused "John Jones"; both Houston dispatches call him Wyatt Jones. The Tombstone dispatch carries a dateline printed as August 18, though the Dallas Herald had reported the capture by August 14.

The 'people of Lynchburg' and an 'excited populace' sought to lynch Jones over a rape accusation (A1, A2), but no one was killed; he was jailed in Houston and the sheriff reportedly kept him there to prevent a lynching (A2, A3).
An early state-news item (A1) and two differently worded Houston dispatches (A2, A3) agree on the accusation near Lynchburg, the hunt to lynch Jones, and his capture and jailing in Houston.

accounts.label: State news item
accounts.gist: Lynchburg would have 'a lynching bee' if the excited populace could run down John Jones, who had raped a white girl the day before; she was found unconscious.

accounts.label: Houston special (Dallas Herald)
accounts.gist: Wyatt Jones, who 'raped' Miss Northcoutt a week earlier, was captured by Black men at Stafford Point and jailed; Lynchburg people had hunted him to lynch him; he denied the crime but acknowledged being the man accused.

accounts.label: Houston dispatch (Tombstone)
accounts.gist: Jones was brought in tied to a horse by two Black men; he told a correspondent he was innocent and had fled for fear of lynching over a suspicion of adultery; the sheriff would probably hold him in Houston.

accounts.label: Jones's own statement
accounts.gist: As reported by the Houston correspondent, Jones said he was innocent and had run away fearing lynching over a suspicion that he had committed adultery.

framing.detail: A one-sentence State News item anticipated 'a lynching bee' by 'the excited populace' without comment and stated the rape as fact.
The Houston special called Jones 'a negro brute' who 'raped' the girl, yet reported the hunt to lynch him without endorsement and noted his denial.
Under the headline 'Strapped to a Horse', the dispatch used 'charged with', printed Jones's own account, and reported the sheriff's fear of a lynching.
The Dallas Weekly Herald reprinted the daily's Houston special unchanged.

conflicts.note: The two Houston dispatches agree on Wyatt; the Aug. 7 brief, before his capture, called him John.

Near Lynchburg, on the bank of the San Jacinto River; capture near Stafford's Point, twenty-five miles from Houston; jailed in Houston.
Wyatt Jones, described as 'a negro' (named 'John Jones' in the earliest report).
Accused of raping a white girl, Miss Northcoutt (also Northcott, Norsecutt), given as 16 years old; she was reported found unconscious.
'The people of Lynchburg' / 'the excited populace', who hunted Jones to lynch him.
